what_its_for: Bupropion is used to treat depression and seasonal affective disorder (SAD), which is depression that comes on during certain times of the year. It is also used to help people quit smoking (sold as Zyban for this purpose). It works by affecting certain chemicals in your brain called dopamine and norepinephrine that help regulate your mood and behavior.
how_to_take: Take bupropion exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow extended-release (SR or XL) tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or split them, as this can cause too much medicine to be released at once. You can take bupropion with or without food, but taking it with food may help if it upsets your stomach. Try to take it at the same time(s) each day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not suddenly stop taking bupropion without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your condition and needs. Common starting doses are 100–150 mg once or twice daily, and your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time. The maximum dose is usually 450 mg per day. For the extended-release (XL) version, it is typically taken once daily in the morning. For the twice-daily (SR) version, doses should be taken at least 8 hours apart to lower the risk of seizures. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time of your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time or double up to make up for a missed dose, as this raises your risk of having a seizure.
storage: Store bupropion at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you no longer need this medication, dispose of it safely — ask your pharmacist about drug take-back programs in your area.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking bupropion, as it can increase your risk of having a seizure. Do not use bupropion if you are also taking or have recently stopped taking MAO inhibitors (such as phenelzine, selegiline, or tranylcypromine) — wait at least 14 days between these medicines. Do not use two bupropion products at the same time (for example, Wellbutrin and Zyban together). Avoid recreational drugs and stimulants. Be careful driving or operating machinery until you know how bupropion affects you, as it can cause dizziness. Do not stop bupropion suddenly without your doctor's guidance.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or call 911 if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm, new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual changes in mood or behavior, a seizure, severe headache, confusion, rapid heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction (rash, itching, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing). Also tell your doctor if you develop high blood pressure, vision changes, or feel like you might faint. Call your doctor if you have any side effects that bother you, including dry mouth, trouble sleeping, headache, nausea, or dizziness. In the first few weeks of treatment, watch closely for any unusual changes in thoughts or feelings, especially in children, teens, and young adults.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your sleep, energy, and appetite within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks of regular use to feel the full benefit for depression. For smoking cessation, you typically start taking bupropion 1 to 2 weeks before your planned quit date. Be patient and continue taking your medicine even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Bupropion is not approved for use in people under 18 years old for depression. If prescribed, close monitoring for suicidal thoughts is required, especially in the first few weeks. Older Adults (65+): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and confusion. Lower doses may be used. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking bupropion if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. The risks and benefits should be discussed carefully. Breastfeeding: Bupropion passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medication. Kidney or Liver Problems: Your doctor may prescribe a lower dose if you have kidney or liver disease. People with Eating Disorders: Bupropion should NOT be used if you have or have had bulimia or anorexia nervosa, as it greatly increases seizure risk in these patients. Seizure History: Tell your doctor if you have ever had a seizure — bupropion may not be safe for you.
